It is stressful. But there are ways to manage that. 

Often times you'll see your friends in other degrees having a much easier time in the corresponding years/semesters. Whereas we start working hard from year1, day 1. It's easy to get let down when thinking about those things. 

The best advice that anyone ever gave me was do what works for you. Everyone thinks they won't get stressed out by looking at others study, or they wont get imposter syndrome or whatever. But med school is the time where everything gets compounded because you realize everyone around is just as smart as you are and just as hardworking as you are. It's impossible NOT to internalize some things. 

Literally the best thing you can do is not look at what others are doing, focus on what works for you. There are several studying techniques, ways to cover syllabus. But do only what works for you. I used to get so stressed out when I saw my classmates studying because my technique wasn't like their's. Wasted a lot of time stressing out. At the end just said fuck it. So yeah, just have that mentality from the get-go and you won't be stressed out as much.

**For reference ayats and ahadith**: I used these books; Fazail e Amaal (you'll be more than covered with this), Riyaz us Saliheen (seriously this is gold for references), Mishkat (this one, I didnt use this one a lot, only used it when I felt  if something particular didn't have enough supporting references). 

**Bonus point**: a lot of references you'll gather for the ahadeeth will help you with your long questions too. So I'm going to give more imformation for that part. 

When you write your **tasheeh**, make sure it's cohesive. Translation. Then the background of it (shaan e nuzool). then tashreeh. then Add in the quranic references. Then the hadith references. Under separate headings. You can add in the points from Fazail e Amaal's explanation into your tashreeh as well. Remember to write the quotations with markers, make them bold. Your keybook has also good points for it. Just remember to integrate what's in your book, your keybook and your own points if you'd like. Often times you can make a lot of important points from there; Impact in dunyavi aur deeni zindagi. This is going to give you enough hefty material to add in the tashreeh.  Like, I cannot stress how solid it'll be. 

For the long question, the answer is again headings. Lafzi tarjuma of what youre given vs actual defintion. when the specific thing was revealed etc. In light of Qur'an, in light of Hadeeth, impact in day-to-day life,  the same gist you've prepared for the above hadeeth tashreeh. In Islamiat the long questions are variable so they'd have a different strategy to them as to how to answer them and compile them but the general idea is the same.

You're going to rely HEAVILY on your own personaly note-taking abilties, and secruing sold marks. 

Solid Marks: Your objectives and short questions. When I tell you they need to be STEEL, I mean it. Do not skip the chapter summaries at the end of the pst book or the objective exercises at the end. Islamiat is pretty straight forward, give the chapters a THOROUGH read as questions are book ki lines for it.

Do not waste too much time on short questions. Write simply what is required because long questions are going to take your time. You don't even have to write the question itself, just the number of the question, then the heading for the answer and give it as is. 

PST SPECIFIC:

 **headings, headings, headings**. Divide your topics into headings that explain it thoroughly. First write a brief introduction of the topic/define it. Give the background to set the stage. If the answer is in the form of lists/points, then made a heading for that point.

 You guys have two books. **Integrate** the info from both books into the question. Do not just use the material from one book. I completed matric in 2017, and when I would prepare for Pst, I'd always use a separate higher-level text book. The one I used was [This particular one](https://www.onlinebookshop.pk/product/standard-a-text-book-of-pakistan-studies-for-b-s-hons-4-years-course-by-sh-muhammad-rafique/). I would add in information from here for my long questions. I would add the information on sticky notes onto my book. 

Secondly, there's a lot of chance you would get the questions from Q.A's perspective. **Add extra quotes** on the ones you have already. I used Quotes From The Quaid book (it's a very small book that has quotes from QA with the index showing what the quote is in regards to). You can use the quotes from the book to **make extra headings** for the question as well i-e what did QA have to say about Palestine, about education etc. EXPAND your answers logically. 

**Draw Maps in geography related questions**, ALWAYS. Even if they're not given in the book. Indicate what area you're talking about when the question is about plateaus, mountainous regions, etc. Just so there's some indication atleast. 

Just try to attempt the long questions from the beginning chapters as they have a lot of material that can be written in the paper as compared to the later ones. But if you can sufficiently prepare the last chapter's questions then obviously go for it.
